# Cerebellar Pathway Diffusion MRI Measures are Linked to Core Autism Symptoms in Early Adolescents Aged 9 to 11 Years

**Authors:** Melyssa Almeida; Leo Zekelman; Zhou Lan; Jarrett Rushmore; Suheyla Cetin-Karayumak; Fan Zhang; Steve Pieper; Nikos Makris; Alexandra J. Golby; Yogesh Rathi; Lauren J. O’Donnell

## Abstract

In this preregistered study, we used diffusion MRI (dMRI) to characterize the tissue properties of cerebellar pathways in 9–11-year-old early adolescents from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study. We examined fractional anisotropy (FA), mean diffusivity (MD), and number of streamlines (NoS) across five cerebellar pathways—the inferior, middle, and superior cerebellar peduncles, the input and Purkinje fibers, and the parallel fibers—in adolescents with (n = 135) and without (n = 7,276) a parent-reported ASD diagnosis. We further tested whether cerebellar dMRI measures differentially related to core ASD symptom domains of social communication and interaction (SCI) and restricted and repetitive behaviors (RRB). Group comparisons revealed significant differences in cerebellar NoS (Pillai’s trace p = 0.033), driven by greater NoS of the superior cerebellar peduncle in early adolescents with ASD; FA and MD showed no significant group effects. Cerebellar pathway dMRI measures exhibited significant interactions with diagnosis in relation to ASD symptom severity. The superior cerebellar peduncle demonstrated the strongest diagnosis-dependent interaction effects, with the NoS showing markedly stronger associations with both social communication (Δβ = 0.14, p = 0.0019) and restricted and repetitive behaviors (Δβ = 0.21, p < 0.0001) in children with ASD. These findings highlight the superior cerebellar peduncle as a key pathway of structural variability and highlight dMRI measures of the cerebellar pathways as meaningful correlates of ASD symptoms in early adolescence.

## Introduction

The cerebellum is among the most consistently implicated brain structures in Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). Early developmental cerebellar injury has been described as one of the strongest known risk factors for later ASD diagnosis, particularly in clinical cohorts with neonatal cerebellar injury such as prematurity-associated hemorrhage (Limperopoulos et al. 2007; Wang et al. 2014; van der Heijden et al. 2021). Cerebellar structural and functional differences are also evident in individuals with ASD without a history of early injury, including differences in cerebellar volume, Purkinje cell pathology, and disrupted cerebro-cerebellar connectivity (D’Mello and Stoodley 2015; Fatemi et al. 2012; Van Overwalle et al. 2020). Core symptoms of ASD span both motor and social-cognitive domains, including difficulties in social communication and restricted or repetitive behaviors (Maenner et al. 2023; American Psychiatric Association 2013). Although traditionally thought of as a structure involved primarily in motor processes, research has increasingly revealed the cerebellum’s involvement in social, cognitive, and affective processing (D’Mello and Stoodley 2015; Van Overwalle et al. 2020; Schmahmann et al. 2019)—domains that overlap with the core behavioral features of ASD.

The cerebellar pathways form an extensive network of intrinsic and extrinsic connections, integrating the cerebellum with the rest of the central nervous system through multi-synaptic loops linking the cerebrum, brainstem, and spinal cord (Ramnani 2006; Voogd 2003; Larsell and Jansen 1972). Through these connections, the cerebellum is believed to contribute to the coordination and prediction of motor, cognitive, and social processes by modulating activity across distributed brain networks (Schmahmann et al. 2019; Van Overwalle et al. 2020). Disruptions to cerebellar white matter pathways can alter communication between the cerebellum and cortical regions involved in social cognition, executive function, and sensorimotor integration. Such alterations are thought to contribute to core features of ASD, including social communication difficulties, restricted or repetitive behaviors, and motor coordination differences (Fatemi et al. 2012; Stoodley and Limperopoulos 2016; D’Mello and Stoodley 2015). Importantly, the intrinsic cerebellar cortex circuitry—particularly Purkinje cells and their parallel fiber inputs—regulates cerebellar output by modulating activity of the deep cerebellar nuclei, which provide the primary output to cerebro-cerebellar pathways (Middleton and Strick 2000; Ito 2006). Additionally, post-mortem studies have consistently reported Purkinje cell loss or reductions in individuals with ASD, including regionally specific decreases in Purkinje cell number and density, suggesting that disruption of intrinsic pathways may contribute to altered cerebellar connectivity in autism (Bailey et al. 1998; Fatemi et al. 2002; Whitney 2008; Kemper and Bauman 2002). As a result, investigating the microstructural properties of cerebellar white matter pathways may provide insight into neurobiological mechanisms underlying ASD symptom expression. In studies of ASD, cerebellar abnormalities are amongst the most consistent findings, with several studies noting differences in cerebellar structure and connectivity which suggest the importance of cerebellar pathways in the etiology of ASD (D’Mello and Stoodley 2015; Biswas et al. 2024; Fatemi et al. 2012; Bauman and Kemper 1985; Ritvo et al. 1986; Bailey et al. 1998). However, the extent to which the tissue microstructural properties of the cerebellar pathways are altered in individuals with ASD and associated with the core symptoms of ASD remains poorly understood (Stoodley and Limperopoulos 2016; Rodrigues et al. 2025; Stoodley 2016).

Diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) is the only non-invasive method that can be used to quantify and reconstruct the brain’s structural connections (Zhang et al. 2022). dMRI measures the magnitude and directionality of water molecule movement in 3D space, enabling the mapping of cerebellar pathways via tractography (Habas and Manto 2018). Cerebellar dMRI tractography enables the investigation of extrinsic cerebellar connections, specifically the cerebellar peduncles that project to and from the cerebellum. These pathways include the inferior, middle, and superior cerebellar peduncles (Habas and Manto 2018). In addition to these pathways, dMRI tractography enables the examination of intrinsic cerebellar connections, including parallel fibers that extend across the cerebellar cortex, as well as the medullary white matter of the cerebellum, where the dMRI signal reflects both cerebellar input fibers and Purkinje fibers (Zhang et al. 2018; Dell’Acqua et al. 2013; Takahashi et al. 2013; Zekelman et al. 2025). Furthermore, dMRI enables the quantification of cerebellar tissue microstructure through measures such as fractional anisotropy (FA), mean diffusivity (MD), and the number of streamlines (NoS) (Zhang et al., 2022). While FA, MD, and NoS are sensitive to microstructural variation, they are influenced by multiple anatomical features and do not correspond to any single microstructural property (e.g., myelin formation and remodeling, axon diameter, inflammation, organization, and fiber crossing) (Beaulieu 2002; Zhang et al. 2022; Alexander et al. 2019; Zatorre et al. 2012).

Previous dMRI studies have indicated an abnormal microstructure of the cerebellar peduncles in individuals with ASD; however, findings have not been consistent. For example, studies of the superior cerebellar peduncle have shown evidence of both decreased FA (Hanaie et al. 2013; Brito et al. 2009) and no significant differences in FA (Wilkes et al. 2024) when comparing participants with and without ASD. Investigations of the middle cerebellar peduncle have found both increased (Cheng et al. 2010; Sivaswamy et al. 2010; Andrews et al. 2019) and decreased (Ogur and Boyunaga 2015; Shukla et al. 2010) FA in children with ASD. Investigations of the inferior cerebellar peduncle have found decreased FA (Sivaswamy et al. 2010) and decreased MD (Srivastava et al. 2024) associated with an autism diagnosis. Additionally, while some studies have found decreased cerebellar peduncle FA to be associated with elevated behavior problems in ASD (Ogur and Boyunaga 2015), others found no relationship at all between the microstructure measures and clinical symptoms of ASD (Shukla et al. 2010). Adding further complexity, a recent meta-analysis found no significant cerebellar peduncle microstructural differences between individuals with and without ASD, despite observing widespread alterations across the cerebrum (Yoon et al. 2025). Additionally, studies of cerebellar structural connectivity/macrostructure are limited in ASD; however, one small-scale study (n=29) reported decreased NoS in a pathway connecting the cerebellar cortex to the dentate nuclei in children with ASD (Jeong et al. 2014). While previous dMRI studies have investigated the parallel fibers that extend across the cerebellar cortex (Zhang et al. 2018; Dell’Acqua et al. 2013; Takahashi et al. 2013; Zekelman et al. 2025), the parallel fibers have not yet been specifically investigated in ASD populations.

Thus, it remains unclear how cerebellar microstructure and macrostructure may be altered in ASD populations and how it may relate to ASD symptoms. Inconsistent findings may be due to numerous reasons. First, many previous cerebellar investigations of individuals with ASD have relied on small sample sizes of 30 or fewer ASD participants (Kilroy et al. 2022; Yoon et al. 2025; Travers et al. 2012; Hanaie et al. 2013). Given the considerable heterogeneity of ASD, small sample sizes can yield unstable results (Travers et al. 2012; Yoon et al. 2025). Second, previous studies have often included a relatively wide age range of children and adolescents with ASD, which, coupled with small sample sizes, may limit the ability to characterize cerebellar macro- and microstructural features specific to early adolescence (Leisman et al. 2025).

Late childhood and the transition into early adolescence represent a valuable window for investigating the cerebellum in ASD because the human cerebellar pathways follow a protracted developmental trajectory that may extend into adolescence (Olson et al. 2023; Haldipur et al. 2022). This prolonged development may predispose the cerebellum to abnormalities in synaptic structure and function, which can culminate in early childhood and progress into adulthood (Muehlbacher et al. 2025; Fatemi et al. 2025; Tiemeier et al. 2010). As such, studying 9–11-year-old early adolescents, provides a critical opportunity to examine how cerebellar development relates to ASD and associated symptom expression. Few previous dMRI studies of ASD have focused on the adolescent age range (Cheng et al. 2010; Shukla et al. 2010; Groen et al. 2011).

To further our understanding of how ASD may impact the microstructural anatomical components of the cerebellar pathways in 9–11-year-old early adolescents, we assessed how the cerebellar microstructure differs between adolescents with and without an ASD diagnosis (n = 135). We also examined the relationship between cerebellar pathway microstructural measures and ASD-associated behaviors, including social communication and interaction, as well as restricted and repetitive behaviors, to gain insight into the potential significance of cerebellar pathway microstructure in ASD. In this study, we utilized diffusion neuroimaging data and behavioral and cognitive scores from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) dataset for 9345 American adolescent children between the ages of 9 and 11 years (mean age = 9.9 ± 0.6 years) (Casey et al. 2018; Volkow et al. 2018; Cetin-Karayumak et al. 2024). The ABCD dataset offers a large cohort drawn from the general population, including children with and without ASD, and excludes individuals with severe sensory, neurological, medical, or intellectual impairments (Thompson et al. 2019). The analytic sample included 135 children with a parent-reported ASD diagnosis and 7,276 comparison participants without ASD after applying study inclusion criteria (see Methods). This study represents a very large comparative investigation of the cerebellar pathways in relation to ASD associated symptoms within a narrow age range of participants with and without ASD.

## Materials & Methods

### Study Overview

This study was pre-registered on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/6ycxz). We compared participants with an ASD diagnosis to participants without an ASD diagnosis using diffusion magnetic resonance imaging to measure fractional anisotropy, number of streamlines, and mean diffusivity of five cerebellar pathways (the inferior, middle, and superior cerebellar peduncles, the medullary white matter (composed of input & Purkinje fibers), and the parallel fibers). Our preregistered hypotheses centered on FA as the primary measure of interest. We tested whether individuals with an ASD diagnosis differed from comparison participants in FA across the five pathways, and whether Social Responsiveness Scale symptom scores for social communication and interaction (SCI) and restrictive repetitive behaviors (RRB) were more strongly associated with FA in the five pathways in the ASD group than in the comparison group. We additionally examined NoS and MD on an exploratory basis to broaden the characterization of cerebellar pathway alterations associated with ASD diagnosis and symptom severity.

### ABCD Dataset Overview

The ABCD Study is a longitudinal, multi-site study into brain and cognitive development and child health (Jernigan et al. 2018). The participants, along with their caregivers, participated in a baseline visit that included completing questionnaires and neurocognitive interviews and undergoing a neuroimaging protocol. From the baseline timepoint, we studied a parent-reported ASD diagnosis from the initial ABCD enrollment screening form and a harmonized and processed dMRI ABCD dataset, which comprises quality-controlled imaging data and extracted dMRI measures from 9,345 ABCD participants aged 9 to 11 years (Cetin-Karayumak et al. 2024). Additionally, we utilized the short Social Responsive Scale, which was administered one year after baseline data collection (Barch et al. 2018). The ABCD1 and harmonized and processed dMRI ABCD2 datasets are available at the National Institute of Mental Health Data Archive.

### Participant Groups

This study examined two groups of participants from the harmonized and processed dMRI ABCD dataset: (1) children with a parent-reported diagnosis of ASD and (2) a comparison group without a parent-reported ASD diagnosis. The ABCD Study includes a large community sample of early adolescents from across the USA. The ABCD Study screening criteria excluded children who did not attend regular school classes, children who were diagnosed with an intellectual disability, a serious medical, or neurological condition (e.g., stroke, cerebral palsy, brain tumor, brain aneurysm, brain hemorrhage, subdural hematoma), and children who experienced one or more seizures per month when taking medication (NIMH Data Archive, n.d.). Additionally, the ABCD Study screening criteria included participants who were reported by their parents to be able to work with the research team, complete questions and puzzles on an iPad, follow directions, and remain still during MRI scanning (NIMH Data Archive, n.d.). As a result, individuals with more severe ASD-related impairments are likely underrepresented. Participants missing behavioral data or parent-reported ASD diagnosis data were excluded from analyses (n = 536; Figure 1). ASD status was determined via parent report at enrollment, identifying 135 participants with an ASD diagnosis and 8,464 without. All 135 children with ASD were included in the ASD group (n = 135; 20 female; mean age = 120.13 months ± 7.46), with an average composite cognitive score of 85.35 ± 10.91, as measured by the NIH Toolbox estimates of crystallized and fluid intelligence. Of these, 76 also had another commonly co-occurring diagnosis (e.g., anxiety, ADHD, or depression). Because psychiatric comorbidity is highly prevalent in ASD (Barlattani et al. 2023), these co-occurring conditions were retained in the ASD group to preserve the representativeness of the ASD sample and to remain consistent with prior neuroimaging studies using ABCD data (Sharp et al. 2023; Zeevi et al. 2026; Christensen et al. 2023). For the comparison group, participants with any additional psychiatric diagnosis (e.g., anxiety, depression, ADHD) were excluded, following prior similar studies (Christensen et al. 2023; Huang et al. 2025). This approach was used to create a typically developing comparison group without known neurodevelopmental or psychiatric conditions, allowing differences to be interpreted relative to typical development rather than to other clinical disorders. The resulting comparison group comprised 7,276 children without an ASD diagnosis (3,677 female; mean age = 118.9 months ± 7.53), with a mean composite cognitive score of 87.17 ± 8.70, as measured by the NIH Toolbox. Siblings were included across both the ASD and comparison group to include the maximum number of participants.

### Harmonized ABCD Diffusion MRI Database

The harmonized diffusion MRI dataset was accessed through the National Institute of Mental Health Data Archive (Cetin-Karayumak et al. 2024). The database includes harmonized dMRI data, tractography, extracted white matter tracts, and microstructure measures from the ABCD study. Details about the database follow. First, a robust dMRI data harmonization algorithm (Cetin Karayumak et al. 2019; Cetin-Karayumak et al. 2022, 2024) was applied to remove scanner-specific biases from the multi-site dMRI data. ABCD participants included in this study were imaged across 18 sites in the United States using 3T Siemens and GE scanners with differing software versions (Hagler et al. 2019). Diffusion MRI data were acquired using multiband EPI (slice acceleration factor = 3; 1.7 mm isotropic resolution) with 96 diffusion-weighted directions, seven b=0 images, and four b-values (500, 1000, 2000, and 3000 s/mm2) distributed across 6, 15, 15, and 60 directions, respectively. Repetition/echo times were 4100/88 ms for Siemens scanners and 4100/81.9 ms for GE scanners (Hagler et al. 2019). Because diffusion MRI data were collected across multiple sites using different scanners and acquisition protocols, a retrospective harmonization algorithm was applied to remove scanner- and site-related variability. This harmonization approach operates directly on the diffusion signal to eliminate nonlinear scanner effects while preserving inter-subject biological variability, enabling pooled analysis across sites. Post-harmonization validation experiments demonstrated substantial reduction of inter-scanner bias and improved consistency of diffusion measures across sites, supporting the use of the harmonized dataset for large-scale group analyses (Cetin-Karayumak et al. 2024). Second, robust multi-fiber tractography was computed in the whole brain of all 9345 subjects to consistently trace white matter connections (Reddy and Rathi 2016). This employed the Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF) tractography method, which estimates fiber-specific microstructural properties (Reddy and Rathi 2016). Third, 73 subject-specific anatomical white matter tracts were extracted from the tractography of each subject in an automated fashion, and their fiber-specific microstructural properties were quantified (Zhang et al. 2018). This process used the atlas-based WhiteMatterAnalysis (WMA) approach, which consistently parcellates white matter tracts across the lifespan with high test-retest reproducibility (Zhang et al. 2019, 2018).

### Cerebellar Pathways and dMRI Measures

Five major cerebellar pathways were analyzed in this study: the inferior, middle, and superior cerebellar peduncles, as well as the input and Purkinje fibers and the parallel fibers (Figure 2). Each pathway was studied in both hemispheres to ensure that decussating fibers were not divided across hemispheres. The input and Purkinje fibers encompassed both afferent inputs to the cerebellum (e.g., climbing and mossy fibers) and intrinsic fibers originating from Purkinje cells, which together contribute to the diffusion MRI signal observed within the cerebellar medullary white matter.

For all subjects, tract-specific microstructural measures of FA, MD, and NoS were investigated. These measures have been previously shown to be associated with neurocognitive scores (Zekelman et al. 2022; Madole et al. 2021; Chen et al. 2022). Here, FA and MD are measures of fiber-specific tissue microstructure, while NoS is widely used to quantify the connectivity strength (Zhang et al. 2022).

### Measures of ASD Associated Behaviors

The short Social Responsiveness Scale contains six items corresponding to the DSM-5 symptom domain of SCI and five items corresponding to the DSM-5 symptom domain of RRB, as identified by prior factor analysis (Frazier et al. 2014; Constantino and Gruber 2012). Parents rated the truth of the statements on a scale of 1–4, with higher scores indicating a greater deficit (Table 1). Following the literature, total SCI and RRB symptom severity scores were computed as the sum of ratings for the symptom domain items (Frazier et al. 2014; Schwarzlose et al. 2023). In line with previous research (Agulleiro et al. 2023), participants in the ABCD dataset with ASD scored significantly higher than those without ASD on both the symptom domain scales (see Figure 3). For SCI, the ASD group (M = 13.4, SD = 3.9) scored higher than the non-ASD group (M = 7.7, SD = 1.9), t(135.2) = −16.9, p < 0.001, 95% CI [−6.4, −5.0]. Similarly, for RRB, the ASD group (M = 11.24, SD = 3.5) scored higher than the non-ASD group (M = 5.95, SD = 1.6), t(135.1) = −17.4, p < 0.001, 95% CI [−5.9, −4.7]. These results indicate significant behavioral differences between participants with and without an ASD diagnosis.

### Statistical Analyses

We examined potential microstructural differences across cerebellar pathways between 9–11-year-old early adolescents with and without an ASD diagnosis. For each diffusion MRI measure (FA, MD, and NoS), a one-way multivariate analysis of covariance (MANCOVA) was performed, treating the five pathway values as multivariate response variables. Primarily, we are interested if the response variables are altered by ASD diagnosis. Age, sex, head motion, and composite cognitive score are considered as additional covariates in the MANCOVA model, following ABCD guidelines and prior ASD investigations (Hagler et al. 2019; DiPiero et al. 2023). To reduce recruitment biases in the ABCD dataset, propensity weights obtained from the ABCD dataset were applied as design weights in adjusted models (see Supplementary Figure 1 for distribution of propensity weights) (Heeringa and Berglund 2020). These weights were derived using inverse-probability weighting procedures that calibrate the ABCD sample to match national distributions of demographic and socioeconomic characteristics from the American Community Survey, allowing estimates to better approximate the U.S. population of children rather than the recruited ABCD cohort alone (Heeringa and Berglund 2020). The weighting procedure incorporated demographic and socioeconomic variables, including child age, sex, and race/ethnicity, as well as family income, family type, household size, caregiver employment status, and U.S. Census region. Consistent with ABCD analytic guidelines (Gard et al. 2023), weights were applied in adjusted models to improve population-level inference. For each model, omnibus significance was assessed using Pillai’s trace (Pillai 1955). When a significant main effect of diagnosis was observed, we conducted post hoc pairwise comparisons to determine which specific cerebellar pathways differed between groups.

To better understand the relationship between cerebellar pathway dMRI measures and ASD symptom domains, we examined how an ASD diagnosis and FA, MD, and NoS of the cerebellar pathways were associated with measures of SCI and RRB using multiple linear regression. A total of 30 regression models (5 cerebellar pathways ✕ 3 diffusion MRI measures ✕ 2 ASD symptom domains) were fit, where each model examined associations between cerebellar pathway diffusion MRI measures and ASD symptom severity, and tested whether these associations differed by ASD diagnosis. SCI and RRB scores were considered dependent variables. Cerebellar dMRI measures and ASD diagnosis were our predictor variables, which were incorporated in the regression models as a single interaction variable. We examined this interaction effect between the two predictor variables to test whether the relationships between dMRI measures and ASD symptom domains differed between participants with and without an ASD diagnosis. Additionally, all models included age, sex, head motion, and composite cognitive score as covariates. Multiple-comparison correction was applied across the five cerebellar pathways within each symptom domain and diffusion measure, consistent with our a priori focus on pathway-specific effects (Lindquist and Mejia 2015). FA, MD, and NoS were analyzed separately because they capture distinct aspects of diffusion MRI tractography and are not directly interchangeable measures of cerebellar pathways (Zhang et al. 2022). Accordingly, each diffusion measure was treated as a separate outcome family for statistical correction, with FA representing the primary hypothesized measure and MD and NoS serving as exploratory analyses.

All analyses were conducted in R version 4.3.1, a language and environment for statistical computing (R: A Language and Environment for Statistical Computing. Preprint at R Foundation for Statistical Computing 2023). Standardized regression coefficients were computed using the ‘lm.beta’ package in R (Behrendt 2023). Cerebellar visualizations were created in 3D Slicer with SlicerDMRI (Norton et al. 2017).

## Results

### Significant Differences in NoS of SCP Across 9–11-Year-Old Early Adolescents With and Without ASD Diagnosis

The MANCOVA analysis indicated a significant group difference in pathway NoS (p = 0.033*) (Table 2). Additionally, in the adjusted MANCOVA, all added covariates were significant (p < 0.0001***; Table 2). Post-hoc analysis again identified the SCP as the only pathway showing significant effects, with participants with ASD exhibiting greater NoS than participants in the comparison group without an ASD diagnosis (p = 0.0012**) (Table 3). No significant group differences emerged for the MCP, ICP, PF, or IP (all p > 0.05). Figure 4 displays NoS across cerebellar pathways for adolescents with and without an ASD diagnosis. Overall, group differences in NoS were specific to the SCP, with no significant effects observed in the other pathways. Together, these findings suggest that altered SCP connectivity may represent a key cerebellar pathway difference in 9–11 year old early adolescents with ASD, independent of demographic and behavioral factors.

### No Significant Differences in Fractional Anisotropy and Mean Diffusivity Across 9–11-Year-Old Early Adolescents With and Without ASD Diagnosis

In contrast to the NoS findings, FA did not differ significantly between groups in the adjusted MANCOVA (p = 0.31) (Supplementary Figure 2). Analysis of MD across pathways revealed no significant differences across pathways in the adjusted MANCOVA (p = 0.13) (Supplementary Figure 3). Additional details are provided in Supplementary Figures 2 and 3, as well as Supplementary Tables 1 and 2. Overall, these null findings for FA and MD highlight that group differences were specific to cerebellar pathway NoS rather than microstructural measures.

### Diagnosis-Dependent Cerebellar–Symptom Associations

To test whether associations between cerebellar pathway dMRI measures and symptom severity differed by ASD diagnosis, we fit propensity-weighted linear models with a diagnosis interaction term, adjusting for age, sex, head motion, and cognitive ability (for additional details see Materials and Methods, Statistical Analyses). As shown in Figure 5, several pathways, most notably the superior and inferior cerebellar peduncles and the input and Purkinje fibers, and parallel fibers, showed significant diagnosis-related differences in associations between dMRI measures and symptom severity. We report standardized beta coefficients and p-values corrected for multiple comparisons. Note, Figure 5 plots model-adjusted linear fits and their corresponding fitted values. For a visualization of the variance of the unadjusted data, see corresponding Supplementary Figure 4).

Across models with a significant interaction with diagnosis (Figure 5), associations between cerebellar pathway dMRI measures and symptom severity were consistently small among 9–11-year-old early adolescent participants without ASD, whereas both positive and negative relationships emerged in participants with ASD. Positive interactions between NoS and symptom severity were most robust: greater NoS in the superior and inferior cerebellar peduncles and in the input and Purkinje fibers was linked to higher SCI and/or RRB scores in participants with ASD, with near-zero slopes in participants without ASD. In contrast, microstructural measures of a few pathways showed negative interactions: greater FA of the parallel fibers was associated with lower SCI scores, and greater MD of the inferior cerebellar peduncle was associated with lower RRB scores, again with negligible associations in early adolescent participants without ASD. Collectively, these findings show that dMRI measures of the cerebellar pathways relate to symptom severity in a diagnosis-dependent manner, with markedly stronger associations in participants with ASD than in those without this diagnosis.

dMRI measures of two cerebellar pathways, the superior and inferior cerebellar peduncle, showed significant interactions with ASD diagnosis consistently for both SCI and RRB measures of symptom severity (left and right panels of Figure 5, respectively). The NoS of the superior cerebellar peduncle showed a significant positive interaction with diagnosis consistently across both symptom domains (SCI: Δβ = 0.14, 95% CI [0.06, 0.23], p = 0.0019; RRB: Δβ = 0.21, 95% CI [0.13, 0.30], p < 0.0001). Additionally, there were significant interaction findings for the inferior cerebellar peduncle in both SCI and RRB symptom domains: (i) NoS of the inferior cerebellar peduncle was differently associated with SCI symptom severity across participants with and without ASD (Δβ = 0.12, 95% CI [0.056, 0.18], p < .001), and (ii) MD of the inferior cerebellar peduncle was differently associated with RRB symptom severity in participants with and without ASD (Δβ = −0.90, 95% CI[−0.36, −0.90], p < 0.01). Thus, we observe consistency across symptom domains in how dMRI measures of the superior and inferior cerebellar pathways relate to symptom severity, highlighting the potential importance of these pathways in the neurobiological basis of ASD associated behaviors.

In 24 of the 30 models studied, diagnosis interactions were not significant (p > 0.05 after correction for multiple comparisons, Supplementary Figure 5 and Supplementary Table 3). In particular, FA, MD, and NoS of the middle cerebellar peduncle showed no significant interactions with diagnosis for either symptom domain, suggesting that microstructural variation in this peduncle may play a limited role in ASD-related behaviors in early adolescent children.

Additionally, although NoS of the superior cerebellar peduncle consistently showed a significant positive interaction with diagnosis across both symptom domains, neither FA nor MD of this pathway exhibited significant diagnosis interactions. This aligns with our MANCOVA results above, which revealed a significant difference in NoS—but none in FA or MD—between early adolescents with and without ASD. Notably, these group-level NoS differences were primarily driven by greater NoS of the superior cerebellar peduncle in early adolescents with ASD. Overall, results indicate that ASD-related differences in cerebellar dMRI measures are pathway-specific, with the superior cerebellar peduncle showing the strongest diagnostic differentiation—both at the group level and in its associations with ASD-related symptoms.

## Discussion

### Overview of Findings

The present study examined cerebellar white matter microstructure (FA, MD) and connectivity (NoS) in 9–11-year-old early adolescents with and without a parent-reported ASD diagnosis using dMRI, and related these measures to dimensional ratings of SCI and RRB. We found that the NoS in the superior cerebellar peduncles was significantly higher in early adolescents with ASD and was shown to increase with symptom severity in this group. However, we did not find group differences in FA, in contrast to our preregistered hypothesis that individuals with an ASD diagnosis would differ in FA of the five cerebellar pathways of interest. Additionally, our findings implicate the parallel fibers, input & Purkinje fibers, and inferior cerebellar peduncles in the symptoms of ASD. These findings underscore the cerebellum’s contribution to core ASD symptom domains and highlight specific pathways that may reflect neurobiological mechanisms underlying symptom variability.

### Superior Cerebellar Peduncles

A central result of this study was the increased NoS in the superior cerebellar peduncles among 9–11-year-old early adolescents with ASD (Fig. 4). Prior research examining FA and MD in this pathway has yielded mixed results, with some studies reporting reduced FA (Kleinhans et al. 2012; Brito et al. 2009; Hanaie et al. 2013) or increased MD (Sivaswamy et al. 2010). In our sample, we observed no significant differences in FA or MD across any cerebellar pathway (Supplementary Figs. 2, 3), a finding consistent with recent meta-analytic evidence showing that neither FA nor MD in the cerebellar peduncles differ significantly between individuals with and without ASD (Yoon et al. 2025). It is important to note that while NoS may be influenced by many neuroanatomical components (e.g., number of neurons, axonal density, diameter of pathway, etc.), it is not a direct index of any single neuroanatomical component and is influenced by diffusion MRI acquisition and processing parameters (Zhang et al. 2022), reducing its biological interpretability (Jones et al. 2013; Zhang et al. 2022) (Jones et al. 2013). Despite these methodological considerations, elevated NoS has also been reported in other ASD-relevant regions, such as the fronto-temporal and basal ganglia (Conti et al. 2017; Pugliese et al. 2009), suggesting that increased streamline counts may reflect aspects of atypical neuroanatomy observable in diffusion-based reconstructions.

The superior cerebellar peduncles were also implicated in ASD symptom severity: higher NoS was associated with greater SCI and RRB symptoms in participants with ASD (Fig. 5). Prior work relating cerebellar volume to ASD symptoms has similarly found that greater symptom severity may accompany larger cerebellar volumes (Elandaloussi et al. 2023; McKinney et al. 2022; Pote et al. 2019). The superior cerebellar peduncles have traditionally been examined in the context of motor coordination differences in ASD (Kilroy et al. 2022; Hanaie et al. 2013), yet our findings demonstrate involvement in both symptom domains, linking this pathway to social communication differences as well as repetitive behaviors. This pattern aligns with broader evidence that the cerebellum influences not only motor but also cognitive, affective, and social functions (D’Mello and Stoodley 2015; Stoodley 2016). Additionally, the literature also describes both functional hyper- and hypoconnectivity of cerebellar networks in ASD (Haghighat et al. 2021; Lanciano et al. 2025; Su et al. 2021), potentially reflecting age-dependent organization; adolescence may represent a developmental period during which connectivity shifts occur, although the precise timing and directionality of these changes remain to be clarified (Shan et al. 2025; Haghighat et al. 2021).

### Biological Dissociability and Overlap of Symptom Domains

Beyond the superior cerebellar peduncles, several additional pathways showed associations with SCI, suggesting that social communication differences may arise from alterations in specific cerebellar pathways. Partially in line with our initial hypothesis that SCI and RRB scores would be more strongly associated with FA in the ASD group, we found higher SCI scores in 9–11-year-old early adolescents with ASD were associated with increased NoS in the input & Purkinje fiber system and decreased FA in the parallel fibers. However, contrary to our initial preregistered hypothesis, the remaining pathways showed no significant FA associations (Fig. 5). These findings are consistent with extensive animal research implicating Purkinje cell dysfunction in social impairments and suggest that microstructural variation in cerebellar cortical pathways may contribute to individual differences in social functioning (Reith et al., 2013; Tsai et al., 2012; van der Heijden et al., 2021; Yamashiro et al., 2020). In contrast, these pathways did not relate to RRB scores (Fig. 5), pointing to a degree of biological dissociability between symptom domains consistent with recent studies that have suggested that specific ASD symptoms, such as SCI and RRB, while co-occurring, may each have distinct genetic patterns and neural correlates (Litman et al., 2025; Warrier et al., 2019).

At the same time, our results also support partial overlap in the neural correlates of SCI and RRB. dMRI measures of the inferior and superior cerebellar peduncles were associated with both domains, implying that some cerebellar pathways may contribute broadly to ASD symptomatology. In particular, we found that in participants with ASD, higher SCI scores were associated with increased NoS in the inferior cerebellar peduncles, while higher RRB scores were related to reduced MD in this pathway (Fig. 5). Prior studies have linked inferior cerebellar peduncle microstructure to social deficits (Ramphal et al. 2021) and to sensory features —sensory abnormalities being a key component of the RRB domain (Surgent et al. 2022). These converging associations suggest that brainstem–cerebellar communication may support multiple behavioral dimensions, while more localized intrinsic cerebellar cortical circuits may relate predominantly to social communication.

### Neuropathological Context

Neuropathological changes in the cerebellum of autistic individuals were first described in the 1980s (Williams et al. 1980; Bauman and Kemper 1985; Ritvo et al. 1986) and have been extended by subsequent postmortem investigations (Bailey et al. 1998; Kemper and Bauman 1993; Whitney et al. 2008; Wegiel et al. 2014; Skefos et al. 2014). Early case reports suggested that Purkinje cell loss was largely restricted to cerebellar hemispheric territories (Bauman and Kemper 1985; Kemper and Bauman 1993), whereas later studies demonstrated considerable variability in the spatial distribution of Purkinje cell loss across the cerebellum (Ritvo et al. 1986; Bailey et al. 1998; Whitney et al. 2008).

More recent work using unbiased stereological methods and accounting for confounding factors such as epilepsy identified selective Purkinje cell loss in Crus I and Crus II (Whitney et al. 2008). These cerebellar cortical regions have been found to participate in cerebro-cerebellar circuits with the prefrontal cortex (Schmahmann and Pandya 1995; Strick et al. 2009) and have been implicated in social cognition and interaction (Van Overwalle et al. 2020), providing convergent biological support for the selective associations between cerebellar cortical pathways and SCI observed in the present study.

In contrast, direct anatomical research on the cerebellar peduncles in autism remains sparse. The inferior cerebellar peduncle conveys afferent signals from the ipsilateral spinal cord and the contralateral inferior olivary nucleus. Notably, Bauman and Kemper reported that the inferior olivary nucleus in autistic adults did not show retrograde cell loss proportional to Purkinje cell loss (Bauman and Kemper 1985; Kemper and Bauman 1993), a finding supported by later work (Wegiel et al. 2014). Bailey et al. (1998) identified ectopic neurons in and adjacent to the inferior cerebellar peduncles in a small number of cases, but no consistent abnormalities have been reported across studies. There are no anatomical observations in autistic brains concerning the middle cerebellar peduncle.

Similarly, there are no direct neuropathological observations of specific investigations of the superior cerebellar peduncle in autism. This pathway contains efferent axons from neurons in the deep cerebellar nuclei—predominantly the dentate nucleus—with smaller contributions from the emboliform and globose nuclei (Asanuma et al. 1983). In adult autistic brains, these deep nuclei have been reported to exhibit neuronal loss (Bauman and Kemper 1985). In contrast, neurons in the deep nuclei of autistic children were described as enlarged and relatively numerous (Kemper and Bauman 1993). Additional studies found that dentate nucleus neurons were smaller than typical in autistic children but increased in size during adolescence, whereas dentate neurons in control brains decreased in size over the same period (Wegiel et al. 2014). These developmental neuropathological findings may relate to the increased streamline counts in the superior cerebellar peduncles observed in our 9–11-year-old early adolescent ASD sample. However, direct comparisons require unbiased stereological studies quantifying neuron number in the dentate nucleus, which have not yet been conducted.

### Limitations and Implications for Future Research

This study also had potential limitations. Diffusion MRI provides a unique non-invasive approach for tracing and quantifying cerebellar pathways in vivo. However, an important limitation lies in the biological interpretability of the dMRI measures examined here, including FA, MD, and NoS. Although FA and MD have been interpreted in relation to myelin and axonal organization, they are influenced by multiple anatomical features and do not correspond to any single microstructural property (Beaulieu 2002; Alexander et al. 2019; Zhang et al. 2022). Similarly, while NoS is widely used, its precise biological basis remains unclear (Jones et al. 2013; Zhang et al. 2022). Further work is needed to better characterize the neuroanatomical significance of variation in dMRI measures across populations.

In addition, it is important to note that the present study relies on parent-reported ASD diagnosis obtained from the ABCD screener form, rather than a diagnosis that was independently validated within the ABCD Study. In addition, the case–control design was characterized by a substantial imbalance in sample sizes between the ASD and non-ASD groups, with a relatively small number of participants with ASD compared to the large control sample. Although the large control group increases statistical power and the stability of normative estimates, unequal group sizes may influence variance structure and reduce sensitivity to detect smaller effects within the ASD group. Future work examining the neural correlates of ASD could examine measures from the Kiddie Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia for DSM-5 collected at Year 3 of the ABCD Study, which may provide a more accurate characterization of ASD status compared to parent report (Barch et al. 2021; Kaufman et al. 2021; Townsend et al. 2020). Another limitation is that the abbreviated Social Responsiveness Scale, administered by the ABCD study, was used to compute the SCI and RRB scores in this analysis (Table 1). Future studies using validated full-length assessments of SCI and RRB are needed to confirm results. Additionally, the short Social Responsiveness Scale was administered to parents one year after the baseline imaging data were collected as part of the ABCD study. However, this is likely to have had a limited impact since autistic traits have been shown to remain stable in early adolescence (Robinson et al. 2011; Martini et al. 2024). Furthermore, because the ABCD study excluded participants with severe intellectual, sensory, and neurological limitations, the ASD sample likely underrepresents individuals with higher support needs and more severe symptom presentations. As a result, the present findings may not fully generalize across the broader autism spectrum. Future studies including more clinically diverse ASD populations will be important for determining whether the observed cerebellar pathway associations extend across the full range of ASD presentations.

### Influence of Co-occurring Psychiatric Diagnoses and Specificity to ASD

Several limitations related to participant group composition should be considered when interpreting these findings. The ASD group included participants with common co-occurring psychiatric diagnoses, whereas the primary comparison group excluded participants with psychiatric conditions in an effort to create a typically developing reference group. Although this approach is consistent with prior ABCD neuroimaging studies (Sharp et al. 2023; Zeevi et al. 2026; Christensen et al. 2023) and reflects the high prevalence of psychiatric comorbidity in ASD (Barlattani et al. 2023; Lai et al. 2019), it also introduces the possibility that some observed cerebellar pathway differences may reflect shared neurobiological features across neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions rather than ASD-specific alterations alone. To address this concern, we conducted a sensitivity analysis (see Supplementary Information, Common Diagnoses Sensitivity Analysis and Supplementary Table 4) that added an additional 1188 participants with common psychiatric diagnoses to the comparison group. In this analysis, the effect of ASD diagnosis on cerebellar pathway NoS was attenuated and no longer statistically significant (p = 0.053). This suggests that the observed cerebellar pathway NoS differences of the main analysis may partially reflect neurobiological features shared across ASD and other common psychiatric conditions, rather than being entirely specific to ASD alone. These findings underscore the importance of considering psychiatric comorbidity when interpreting neuroimaging differences associated with ASD and suggest that future work should move beyond treating psychiatric comorbidity as a single, heterogeneous construct. Specific co-occurring diagnoses may contribute differentially to cerebellar pathway alterations observed in ASD. For example, ADHD is highly prevalent among children with ASD (Simonoff et al. 2008) and future work should further investigate the effects of co-occurring ADHD and ASD. Although a single variable indicating ADHD diagnosis is not available in the ABCD dataset at this timepoint, prior work has proposed approaches to estimate ADHD prevalence by leveraging multiple operational definitions within the dataset collected at multiple timepoints (Cordova et al. 2022). Future studies incorporating larger ASD samples and dimensional assessments of psychiatric symptoms may help clarify the specificity, developmental timing, and clinical significance of cerebellar pathway alterations across neurodevelopmental conditions.

### Sex Imbalance

In line with previous investigations of ASD (Werling and Geschwind 2013), there is a strong male bias in ASD prevalence within the analyzed ABCD Study cohort; of the 135 participants in the ASD group, only 20 are female (~15%), whereas approximately half of the participants in the comparison group are female. We retained the full sample in order to maximize statistical power and to take advantage of the large and demographically diverse ABCD cohort, which was designed to provide a broadly representative sample of U.S. youth (Garavan et al. 2018; Casey et al. 2018); however, this resulted in an unequal sex distribution between groups, which represents a limitation of the present study. Consistent with prior neuroimaging studies of ASD (Sharp et al. 2023; Walsh et al. 2021), we tested the presence of potential sex effects by including a diagnosis-by-sex interaction term across models. These interaction terms were not significant, suggesting that the association between ASD diagnosis and cerebellar measures was not significantly moderated by sex in this 9–11-year-old early adolescent sample, although the relatively small number of females with ASD limits the power to detect sex-specific effects. Recent work has emphasized the importance of improving sex balance in neuroimaging studies of ASD (Nordahl 2023), and future studies with larger samples of females with ASD will be important for more fully characterizing potential sex-specific effects.

## Conclusion

This study demonstrates that cerebellar white matter pathways are closely related to core ASD symptom domains during the transition from late childhood to early adolescence. Using diffusion MRI, we found that the number of streamlines in the superior cerebellar peduncles was increased in 9–11-year-old early adolescents with a parent-reported ASD diagnosis and scaled with the severity of both social communication impairments and restricted and repetitive behaviors, whereas fractional anisotropy and mean diffusivity did not differ between groups. In addition, cerebellar cortical pathways—including the input & Purkinje fibers and parallel fibers—were selectively associated with social communication impairments, while the inferior cerebellar peduncles were implicated across both symptom domains, indicating both dissociable and shared cerebellar contributions to ASD symptomatology. The selective sensitivity of streamline-based measures is consistent with neuropathological evidence of atypical cerebellar development in autism and suggests that altered cerebellar circuit organization, rather than uniform white matter microstructural disruption, underlies these associations. Together, these findings highlight cerebellar white matter pathways, particularly the superior cerebellar peduncles, as key contributors to ASD symptom variability and important targets for future developmental and longitudinal research.
